lessons.title: Bonus Shares, Splits, Rights and Buybacks: How Corporate Actions Affect Your Tax

body.text: Most corporate actions do not create tax on the day they happen. They quietly reshape your cost and your holding dates, and the bill shows up when you sell. Understand the reshaping and the bill will never surprise you.

children.text: Siddharth, a 41-year-old architect in Hyderabad, has held a long-term portfolio through Zerodha since 2019. Over the years he has received bonus shares, seen a stock split, been offered rights, tendered shares in a buyback, received Jio Financial Services shares from Reliance and watched his HDFC Ltd shares turn into HDFC Bank shares. His tax P&L now shows costs and dates he does not recognise. This lesson decodes each of them.

children.text: Bonus Shares: Nil Cost, Fresh Clock

markDefs.definition: Free additional shares issued to existing shareholders out of the company's reserves. For tax, their cost is nil and their holding period starts on the allotment date.

children.text: In a 1:1 bonus, you get one free share for every share held, and the share price roughly halves. Your
have a cost of nil and a holding period that starts on the allotment date. Your original shares keep their full cost and their original date. That split creates a trap.

body.caption: Siddharth's 1:1 bonus: 100 shares bought at ₹900, price falls from ₹1,200 to about ₹600 after the bonus, all 200 shares later sold at ₹650 (illustrative)

body.text: A long-term capital loss can only be set off against long-term gains. It cannot reduce a short-term gain. So Siddharth could end up paying 20% on the full short-term gain on his bonus shares while his long-term loss waits for a future long-term gain. Chapter 5 covers set-off rules in detail. If you plan to sell after a bonus, check whether waiting 12 months from allotment makes more sense.

body.title: The Bonus Share Gain
body.prompt: Using Siddharth's example above, his 100 bonus shares have nil cost and are sold 8 months after allotment at ₹650 each. What is his short-term capital gain on the bonus shares, in rupees?
body.explanation: Sale value is 100 × ₹650 = ₹65,000. Cost is nil, so the entire ₹65,000 is a short-term capital gain, taxed at 20% if sold on the exchange with STT.

body.title: Deep Dive: FIFO and the Bonus Stripping Rule

children.text: FIFO decides which shares leave first. In a demat account, your original shares are older than your bonus shares, so if you sell only half your holding after a bonus, the original, high-cost shares are treated as sold first. That usually creates a loss now and leaves the zero-cost bonus shares, with their large future gain, in your account.

Bonus stripping is an anti-avoidance rule in section 94(8) of the 1961 Act, extended to shares from 1 April 2023 and carried into the 2025 Act. If you buy shares or units within three months before the record date of a bonus issue and sell any of the original shares within nine months after the record date while keeping the bonus shares, the loss on the originals is ignored. That ignored loss is instead added to the cost of the bonus shares.

content.text: The rule targets people who buy just before a bonus purely to book an artificial loss. Long-term holders who happened to own the shares well before the record date are not affected.

children.text: Splits and Consolidations: Same Money, More Pieces

A stock split changes the number of shares, not your investment. If Siddharth held 50 shares bought at ₹4,000 each and the company splits each share into 5, he now holds 250 shares at a cost of ₹800 each. Total cost stays ₹2,00,000. The holding period still runs from his original purchase date. A consolidation, where several shares merge into one, works the same way in reverse.

body.title: After the Split
body.question: Nandini bought 20 shares at ₹6,000 each 18 months ago. The company does a 1:10 split. She sells all her shares a week later. Which is correct?
options: Her 200 shares have nil cost and a fresh holding period, so the whole sale value is short-term gain
Her 200 shares cost ₹600 each and are long-term, because the holding period runs from her original purchase
Her 200 shares cost ₹6,000 each and are short-term
The split itself was a taxable transfer, so she already paid tax on it
body.explanation: A split is not a transfer and creates no new cost. Her ₹1,20,000 total cost is spread over 200 shares at ₹600 each, and the 18-month holding period continues, so any gain is long-term.

children.text: Rights Issues: Subscribe or Sell the Entitlement

markDefs.definition: The right to subscribe to new shares at a set price in a rights issue. Credited to your demat account and tradable on NSE and BSE during the rights period. Its cost is nil for existing shareholders.

children.text: In a rights issue, you get a
credited to your demat account. You can use it to subscribe to new shares at the offer price, or sell it on NSE or BSE during the trading window.

columns.label: You Subscribe
points: Cost of rights shares = offer price you paid
Holding period starts on allotment of the rights shares

columns.label: You Sell or Renounce the Entitlement
points: Taxable as a capital gain in that tax year
Cost of the entitlement is nil
Holding period runs from the offer date, so it is almost always short-term
If you let it lapse, there is no gain and no loss

body.title: Cost of a Rights Entitlement
body.textWithBlank: If you sell your rights entitlement on the exchange instead of subscribing, its cost of acquisition is taken as ___.
body.explanation: You did not pay anything for the entitlement, since it came with your existing shares, so its cost is nil and the whole sale price is a short-term capital gain.

children.text: Since April 2025, listed companies can buy back shares only through the tender offer route. You tender shares, and the company accepts a proportion based on the acceptance ratio. Only accepted shares are transferred. Unaccepted shares return to your demat account with their original cost and date, and nothing happens to them for tax. As Chapter 1, Lesson 4 explained, from 1 April 2026 accepted shares are taxed as capital gains for non-promoter shareholders.

body.title: Siddharth Tenders in a Buyback
body.scenario: In November 2026, an IT company announces a buyback at ₹1,900. Siddharth bought his shares in 2023 at ₹1,300 each. He tenders 60 shares and the acceptance ratio turns out to be 20%.
body.prompt: How many shares are actually bought back, what is his capital gain, and what happens to the rest?
body.modelAnswer: At 20%, 12 of his 60 shares are accepted. Gain = 12 × (₹1,900 − ₹1,300) = ₹7,200. He has held them for more than 12 months, so this is a long-term capital gain, taxed at 12.5% above his ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption, which comfortably covers it if he has no other large long-term equity gains. The other 48 shares are returned to his demat account with their original cost and purchase date, and there is no tax on them.

children.text: In a demerger, a company spins off a business into a separate listed company, and you receive shares of the new company. This is not a transfer. Instead, your original cost is divided between the parent and the new company in a ratio the parent company announces, and the new shares carry your original purchase date.

body.caption: Reliance Industries and Jio Financial Services demerger, July 2023 (1 JFS share for every 1 Reliance share)
headers: Cost per Share if Reliance Was Bought at ₹2,179

body.title: How an Original Reliance Cost Is Split After the JFS Demerger

body.text: Companies publish the cost apportionment ratio in a stock exchange filing soon after the demerger. Most brokers update your tax P&L automatically, but it is worth checking once, especially for shares moved between brokers or held from physical certificates.

children.text: When HDFC Ltd merged into HDFC Bank in July 2023, shareholders received 42 HDFC Bank shares for every 25 HDFC Ltd shares. Receiving shares of the merged company in exchange is not a transfer. If Siddharth held 25 HDFC Ltd shares at ₹2,000 each (total ₹50,000), he received 42 HDFC Bank shares with a cost of ₹50,000 ÷ 42 = ₹1,190.48 each, and his holding period still runs from his original HDFC Ltd purchase date.

body.title: After Any Corporate Action in Your Portfolio
steps: Note the record date and allotment date from the company's stock exchange announcement
For bonuses and splits, confirm your broker has recorded the new quantity and adjusted cost correctly
For demergers, find the company's cost apportionment filing and check your tax P&L against it
For rights, decide whether to subscribe or sell the entitlement before the trading window closes
For buybacks, record how many shares were actually accepted and keep the tender confirmation
Before selling soon after a bonus, check how many of your shares are still short-term

points: Bonus issues, splits, rights subscriptions, demergers and mergers are not taxed when they happen
Bonus shares have nil cost and a new holding period, which can split one holding into long-term losses and short-term gains
Splits spread your original cost over more shares without restarting the clock
Selling a rights entitlement is a short-term capital gain with nil cost
In a buyback, only accepted shares are taxed, as capital gains from 1 April 2026
Demergers split your original cost in an announced ratio, and mergers carry your old cost and date into the new shares

Company names are used only to illustrate past corporate actions; share prices and quantities for individual investors are illustrative. Sections and rates reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 for tax year 2026-27. Always check a company's official filings and consult a qualified tax professional before acting.
